#Text=The
#Text= Surprise trees bore a crop in 1913, again in 1914, and 1915, making it
#Text= to the present time not only the most productive but the most profitable
#Text= variety on our place.
#Text=While we did not keep an accurate record of the
#Text= exact yield in 1913 and 1914, some of the trees produced fully five 16
#Text= quart cases in 1913.
#Text=A fair average would perhaps be about four cases
#Text= per tree.
#Text=In 1914 the crop was somewhat lighter, yielding an average of
#Text= three cases per tree.
#Text=This year we picked and sold eighty-five cases,
#Text= which brought us a gross revenue of $79.60.
#Text=We lost part of the crop on
#Text= account of continual rain in the picking season, or we would have had
#Text= fully 100 cases.
#Text=Nine of the trees being in a more sheltered location
#Text= than the other ten held their fruit better during the growing season,
#Text= and produced a relatively heavier crop than the ten that were exposed to
#Text= our fierce winds all summer.
#Text=We have never been able to supply the demand for them, at good prices,
#Text= while other varieties went begging at any kind of a price.
#Text=Among their
#Text= good qualities with us are productiveness, good size, extra fine quality
#Text=and attractive color.
#Text=They are delicious to eat out of hand just as they
#Text= are ripe enough to drop from the tree.
#Text=They are fine for canning,
#Text= preserving or jelly.
#Text=They are practically curculio proof, and have never
#Text= been affected with brown rot as have some other varieties.
#Text=Aphis never
#Text= bothers them, while Terry and some other varieties nearly had the whole
#Text= crop ruined by this pest in 1914.
#Text=The branches form good, strong
#Text= shoulders at the trunk and do not split or break down in heavy storms or
#Text= under their heavy loads of fruit, as the Terry and Forest Garden do.
#Text=The
#Text= flower buds and fruit form as freely on the new growth as on the old
#Text= spurs.
#Text=The crop is therefore about evenly distributed all over the tree,
#Text= and while we picked almost eight cases from one tree this year it did
#Text= not appear to be overloaded, as some varieties frequently are, the
#Text= Surprise tree always being capable of maturing all the fruit that sets.
#Text=We have shipped them 300 miles by freight with perfect success, but we
#Text= pick them from the tree before fully ripe.
#Text=If allowed to ripen on the
#Text= tree they drop badly, which bruises and damages them.
#Text=The trees are
#Text= thrifty, vigorous growers with beautiful glossy foliage that can be
#Text= distinguished from all other varieties.
#Text=You would note on examination of the buds that we have promise of
#Text= another crop next year, but this will depend somewhat on the weather
#Text= during the blooming season.
#Text=We attribute one of the reasons for our
#Text= success with the Surprise plum to the fact that they are planted among
#Text= and alongside of varieties that have the same season of blooming, and
#Text= which undoubtedly are good pollenizers, namely the Bursota, Wolf,
#Text= Ocheeda and Omaha.
#Text=The bloom of Surprise being almost sterile, they
#Text= will not be a success planted alone.
#Text=[Illustration: A Surprise plum tree growing on the place of Prof.
#Text=A.G.
#Text=Ruggles.
#Text=It bore in 1914 four bushels, having been well sprayed with
#Text= arsenate of lead and bordeaux mixture.]
#Text=You will perhaps ask if there are no faults or diseases they are subject
#Text= to, and we will state, for one thing, the fruit drops too easily when
#Text= ripe, and you will either have to pick them before fully matured or find
#Text= a good many of them on the ground.
#Text=They are also occasionally subject to
#Text= blossom blight, which was rather a benefit, as it thinned the crop out
#Text= to about the proper proportion.
#Text=We also had considerable plum pocket and
#Text= fungous growth one season about ten years ago.

#Text=consisted of year old stock (purchased the year preceding and set in
#Text= nursery rows) and included these six varieties: Duchess, Patten  '  s
#Text= Greening, Okabena, Wealthy, Hibernal, Anisim.
#Text=Good growth was made the
#Text= past season and the stock went into winter quarters in good shape.
#Text=However, 20 per cent died, the loss being in this order: Wealthy,
#Text= Anisim, Hibernal, Pattens  '   Greening--Okabena and Duchess were tied for

#Text=In addition to the above, we made a considerable planting
#Text= of small fruits, principally currants and gooseberries, together with a
#Text= limited quantity of blackberries and raspberries.
#Text=Twelve varieties of
#Text= strawberries were set out, each including 100 plants.
#Text=All made a
#Text= splendid growth this season.
#Text=An interesting test is under way in the
#Text= dynamiting work.
#Text=Alternate trees have been set in blasted holes, a stick
#Text= about one and one-half inches long being sufficient to make a hole three
#Text= feet in diameter and perhaps twenty inches in depth.
#Text=It is yet too early
#Text= to measure the results of this work, but owing to the nature of the
#Text= subsoil in this region, we are looking for splendid results.
#Text=With regard
#Text= to the stock secured from the Fruit Farm, we have not been uniformly
#Text= successful.
#Text=Much of the stock seems to be weak and dies readily from
#Text= some cause unknown to us.
#Text=Next season we should be able to render a more
#Text= complete report, as our work will then be fairly started.
#Text=Annual Report, 1915, West Concord Trial Station.
#Text=FRED COWLES, SUPT., WEST CONCORD.
#Text=[Illustration: Fred Cowles at home.]
#Text=Of the new varieties of plums that I received from the Fruit-Breeding
#Text= Farm most all have done well.
#Text=The only one that has borne is No. 21.
#Text=This one had two plums on last season, and several this.
#Text=They were a
#Text= medium size red plum, very good flavor, and seem to come into bearing
#Text= very young.
#Text=No. 17 is a very thrifty grower, but when it bears that will
#Text= tell what it is worth.
#Text=Hansen  '  s plums are doing well, but we believe
#Text= they are more adapted to a better drained soil than we have here, as we
#Text= are on a heavy prairie soil.
#Text=But these varieties are very thrifty and
#Text= bear so young.
#Text=The grapes have all stood the winter with no protection and have not
#Text= killed back any.
#Text=We expect some fruit next season.
#Text=The raspberries that we received have all done well.
#Text=No. 4 seems to take
#Text= the lead for flavor and is a good grower.
#Text=Notwithstanding the cold season our strawberry crop was very good, and
#Text= we are much impressed with No. 3, it is so strong and healthy; it is
#Text= just the plant for the farmer, as it will thrive under most any
#Text= condition.
#Text=I believe it will fight its way with the weeds and come out
#Text= ahead.
#Text=We reported very favorably on the Heritage when it was in bloom, but it
#Text= does not set enough fruit to pay for its space.
#Text=The berries are large
#Text= but very few on my grounds.
#Text=I will discard it.
#Text=Our apple crop was very good, especially Duchess, Wealthy and
#Text= Northwestern Greening.
#Text=We have been trying some of the tender varieties
#Text= top-worked.
#Text=Northern Spy gave us five nice apples on a two year graft.
#Text=We also have Jonathan, Talman Sweet and King David doing well.
#Text=Delicious
#Text= grafted three years ago has not fruited yet.
#Text=This has been a splendid summer for flowers, and they seemed to enjoy
#Text= the damp, cool season, especially the dahlia.
#Text=If you have not tried the
#Text= Countess of Lonsdale you should; it is a cactus dahlia and a very free
#Text= bloomer.
#Text=Everblooming roses did well--we had them in October

#Text= PLANT LICE ON BLOSSOMS.
#Text=--Aphids infesting the apple buds
#Text= appeared in serious numbers during the present season in the Illinois
#Text= University orchards when the buds began to swell.
#Text=They were also
#Text= observed in neighboring orchards.
#Text=In 1914, apple aphids caused serious
#Text= damage in certain counties in Illinois, and some damage was reported
#Text= from many sections of the state.
#Text=The aphids attack the opening buds, the young fruits, the growing
#Text= shoots, and the leaves, sucking the plant juices from the succulent
#Text= parts by means of long, very slender, tube-like beaks, which they thrust
#Text=top to bottom and spray twice each season.
#Text=However, the past season half
#Text= the orchard only was sprayed twice, the other half only once, the second
#Text= spraying being applied about two weeks after the first, when we use lime
#Text= and sulphur only, and then five gallons instead of six, in each tank of
#Text= water.
#Text=We use angle nozzles, the better to direct the spray into the
#Text= calyxes.
#Text=The orchard was mowed twice during the summer, early in June and the
#Text= middle of July.
#Text=A heavy growth of clover covers most of the orchard, and
#Text= none is ever removed, all is left to decay just as it is left by the
#Text= mowers.
#Text=The next thing in line to take our attention is thinning the fruit.
#Text=The
#Text= past season we thinned the Wealthy and top-worked varieties only;
#Text= another season, we expect to carry this work to every tree in the
#Text= orchard.
#Text=The trees were gone over twice in the season, although the bulk
#Text= of the work is done at the first operation.
#Text=We use thinning shears made
#Text= expressly for the purpose.
#Text=By the end of July the trees in many instances were carrying maximum
#Text=from the first crop until the last one of the past season.
#Text=[Illustration: Apples by the carload at Howard Lake.]
#Text=In packing we aim to use the kind of package the market demands.
#Text=The
#Text= crop this season was all barreled.
#Text=The pickers have been on the job long
#Text= enough so that they are as able to discriminate as to what should go
#Text= into a barrel and what should not as I am myself.
#Text=However, our system is
#Text= to always have about twice as many barrels open ready for the apples as
#Text= there are pickers.
#Text=The barrels are all faced one layer at least, and two
#Text= layers if we have the time, and as the pickers come in with
#Text= approximately half a bushel of apples in the picking sack, they swing
#Text= the sack over the barrel, lower it, release the catch and the apples are
#Text= deposited without bruising in any way.
#Text=The next picker puts his in the next barrel, and so on, so that each
#Text= succeeding picker deposits his apples in the next succeeding barrel.
#Text=In
#Text= that way I personally have the opportunity to inspect every half bushel
#Text= of apples, or, I might say, every apple, as a half bushel of apples in a
#Text= barrel is shallow, making inspection a very simple matter.
#Text=When the
#Text=barrels are filled they are headed up, put in the packing shed until
#Text= sufficient have accumulated, and when that point is reached they are
#Text= loaded out, billed to Minneapolis, where practically all our apples have
#Text= been sold for years.
#Text=All fruit up to date has been sold on a commission
#Text= basis, the crop for the past season aggregating five carloads, or
#Text= approximately 800 barrels.
#Text=We feel that we have worked out a fairly good method to handle both our
#Text= trees and our apples, but we have not reached the conclusion that our
#Text= methods in any way guarantee us a crop of apples, although in ten years,
#Text= or since the orchard came into bearing, we have never had a season that
#Text= we did not have a fair crop of apples.
#Text=In 1913 we sold seven carloads,
#Text= in 1914 four carloads, in 1915 five carloads, and the trees as far as
#Text= they are concerned promise us a fair crop for 1916.
#Text=We are working as
#Text= though this is assured, but in the final analysis it is up to the
#Text= weather man.

#Text=Growing Beans and Sweet Corn.
#Text=P.
#Text=B.
#Text=MARIEN, ST.
#Text=PAUL.
#Text=Since it is one thing to grow beans and sweet corn and another to make
#Text= money on them, I think from a market gardener  '  s point of view my heading
#Text= should have been "growing beans and sweet corn at a profit."
#Text=I will talk of beans first, because while the two are planted at about
#Text= the same time, beans make their appearance on the market long before
#Text= sweet corn.
#Text=Beans have a nitrogen gathering power and are therefore a soil-improving
#Text= crop.
#Text=They are to the gardener what clover is to the farmer.
#Text=For early
#Text= beans we have found that sandy soil well fertilized is by far the best.
#Text=If possible it should be sloping toward the south, although we have had
#Text= good success on level land well drained.
#Text=One should have the best seed
#Text= possible, and if you get hold of a good strain of seed that produces
#Text= nice, velvety beans earlier than your neighbor, save as much of that
#Text=found two extra bushels, making eighteen instead of sixteen bushels.
#Text=I
#Text= concluded that someone had despaired of selling them and perhaps had
#Text= poor success in trying to give them away and so forced them on me.
#Text=However we consider we did well on our beans, as the first two pickings
#Text= brought from $2.00 to $3.50 per bushel.
#Text=Now a few words about sweet corn.
#Text=Along about the 6th to the 12th of
#Text= July the truck gardener should load his first sweet corn.
#Text=Sweet corn is
#Text= of American origin, having been developed from field corn, or maize.
#Text=No
#Text= large vegetable is so generally grown throughout the country, the
#Text= markets of the cities taking large quantities, and immense areas being
#Text= grown for canning purposes.
#Text=Seed that fails entirely is not often found, but when one has a good
#Text= strain that produces early corn it is best to save some.
#Text=We generally have sweet corn to sell every day from about the middle of
#Text= July until the first frost.
#Text=To do this we plant every ten days from
#Text= about the 20th of April to the 20th of June.
#Text=Our early variety is the
#Text= Peep-O  '  Day, which is planted about the same time as the early beans.
#Text=We
#Text=also plant the Golden Bantam at this time.
#Text=This is followed by Red Cob
#Text= Cory, Pocahontas and some more Bantam.
#Text=Then about May 15th to 20th we
#Text= plant early and late Evergreen, Bantam and Country Gentleman.
#Text=[Illustration: A load of vegetables at Marien  '  s ready for market.]
#Text=Soil well adapted to common field corn will produce good sweet corn,
#Text= thriving best on well fertilized land.
#Text=Sandy soil is best for the early
#Text= varieties.
#Text=Sweet corn is often grown in drills, but we prefer the hills three feet
#Text= apart, as it is easier to get an even stand, and cultivating both ways
#Text= will push the crop.
#Text=It should be cultivated shallow and never deep
#Text= enough to hurt the roots.
#Text=It is well to hoe it once.
#Text=Sweet corn is one of the few vegetables which is quite free from serious
#Text= injury from either insects or diseases.
#Text=Sweet corn may be divided into three classes: early, medium and late.
#Text=It
#Text= is very important that the various kinds come in as early as possible,

#Text= The summer of 1915 will long be remembered as the summer with no warm
#Text= weather.
#Text=There was a heavy frost the morning of June 10th.
#Text=The season  '  s
#Text= rainfall was very heavy, but trees at the best made only a normal
#Text= growth, and with many varieties, especially of forest trees, the growth
#Text= was much less than the usual growth of even a dry season.
#Text=Some fruit trees blossomed quite early, and the young fruit formed
#Text= during a warm spell, and these trees were heavily loaded with fruit.
#Text=This was especially noticeable with Wealthy, Duchess, Okabena and
#Text= Whitney No. 20 apples, and with some of the Hansen hybrid plums.
#Text=Other
#Text= trees, fully as good bearers, blossomed a few days later and set no
#Text= fruit at all, the frost killing the blossoms while not severe enough to
#Text= harm the fruit already set.
#Text=The cool weather of this past season has probably helped fruit growers
#Text= more than it has hindered them, for had it been as hot as it usually is
#Text= when we have such a tremendous rainfall, blight would most certainly
#Text= have caused much trouble, but as it was we have had practically no
#Text= blight at all.
#Text=This season has again demonstrated very plainly the advantages of
#Text= top-working, such trees making a better growth, and the fruit being more
#Text= even, and less troubled with spots, scab, etc.
#Text=The plums sent to this station the spring of 1913 bore no fruit at all
#Text= this season, but the trees made a fair growth and all appear healthy
#Text= except a few that froze back the winter of 1913-14.
#Text=The plum trees sent from the central station the spring of 1914 made a
#Text= very poor growth that season, owing undoubtedly to the fact that the
#Text= roots were dry when reaching here, but this last season all but one made
#Text= a splendid growth, and one No. 10, to my surprise, produced five plums
#Text= that for beauty and eating qualities would place this variety in the
#Text= front rank with the best in the state.
#Text=We shall watch these trees with
#Text= great interest and will report on their actions as they develop.
#Text=The four trees of No. 1 plum, sent here the spring of 1915 from the
#Text= central station, made a splendid growth, each tree developing fruit buds
#Text= in abundance.
#Text=On November 5th our strawberry beds were all given a mulching with loose
#Text= oat straw for a winter protection.
#Text=The several varieties of grape vines originating at the Minnesota State
#Text= Farm on trial here have all made a vigorous growth.
#Text=We have them all
#Text= pruned and laid on the ground, and we intend to give them no other
#Text= winter protection.
#Text=They are in a sheltered location.
#Text=In spite of the
#Text= various freezes early in the season we got samples of fruit from most of
#Text= the varieties.
#Text=Minnesota No. 8 seems to be the earliest to ripen its
#Text= fruit.
#Text=The wild grape flavor is noticeable in all these varieties.
#Text=The various varieties of plum trees sent here from the State Farm made
#Text= vigorous growth the past season and are looking healthy with the
#Text= exception of Minnesota No. 21.
#Text=Of the five trees of this variety each
#Text= one has a great many galls on the body of the tree.
#Text=It is probably what
#Text= is termed black knot, only the galls have not turned black yet.
#Text=They are
#Text= apparently of too recent growth for that.
#Text=It is probable that we will
#Text= plant other trees in their places next spring.

#Text=The Growing of Vegetables for Canning.
#Text=M.
#Text=H.
#Text=HEGERLE, PRES.
#Text=CANNING FACTORY, ST.
#Text=BONIFACIUS.
#Text=The state authorities, through the Agricultural Farm and other sources,
#Text= are doing good work promoting and encouraging the growing of vegetables,
#Text= but it seems more could be done towards the marketing and conservation
#Text= of these vegetables after they are grown.
#Text=so-called fresh vegetables shipped in from a distance at best require
#Text= several days to make the rounds through the grower, the shipper, the
#Text= jobber, the retailer--to our tables and are really not fresh.
#Text=They have
#Text= become stale, and by coming in contact with different kinds of material
#Text= have lost their delicate flavor.
#Text=Therefore to insure real fresh
#Text= vegetables for our tables, at least during the winter months, we must
#Text= take the canned article.
#Text=All of us remember how most everything in the grocery line was handled
#Text= in bulk, dried fruits, cereals of all kinds, coffee, tea, etc., was
#Text= displayed on the counters, along the aisles and even outside along the
#Text= sidewalk, handled and examined by any one and exposed to dust and flies.
#Text=Just about the same way are vegetables in bulk handled today.
#Text=Where is
#Text= the grocer who would go back to those days, and where is the public that
#Text= would patronize him?
#Text=Mrs.
#Text=Glenzke: What vegetables do you can?
#Text=Mr.
#Text=Hegerle: We can corn; beans, string and wax; apples, tomatoes, etc.
#Text=our fruit--not even the neighborhood boys, as they are our best
#Text= friends.
#Text=What they buy we charge them a good fair price for and never
#Text= fail to give all new customers a few choice samples of best varieties.
#Text=By the latter part of the plum season our big red Wolf River apples
#Text= commence to show up and cook well; also Wealthy and McIntosh commence to
#Text= get ripe enough to eat, and the demand each year has far exceeded the
#Text= supply.
#Text=So far we have had very few poor apples, but we always sort them into
#Text= three grades, the third grade being made up into cider to sell while
#Text= sweet.
#Text=The second grade we sell as such for immediate use.
#Text=The firsts of
#Text= the McIntosh we have sold at $2.00 to $2.50 per bushel, Wealthy,
#Text= Jonathan and Grimes at $1.50 to $2.00, while Wolf, N.
#Text=W.
#Text=Greening,
#Text= Salome, Winesap, Milwaukee, etc., have averaged us $1.25 per bushel.
#Text=We
#Text= are always very careful not to have any bruised, diseased or ill shaped
#Text= specimens in our first grade.
